newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Kazakh leader urges more foreign investment.
newsitem.headline: Kazakh leader urges more foreign investment.

text.p: President Nursultan Nazarbayev said on Thursday that foreign capital was essential to rebuild Kazakhstan and he pledged to create favourable conditions for investors wishing to work in the former Soviet republic.
"We invite you to work together to build a new Kazakhstan and promise to take your interests into account," Nazarbayev told an investment summit in the Kazakh capital Almaty.

The summit -- convened by the government and sponsored by U.S. Chevron Corp -- brought together 80 directors and senior officials from some 50 international firms who have business in Kazakhstan or are looking to invest there.

The president said his vast steppeland country -- the size of Western Europe and with a population of only 16.7 million people -- had set an ambitious goal "to become a highly developed state by the middle of the 21st century".
"To implement this plan, we are giving primary importance to attracting foreign investment and creating favourable conditions for it," he said.
Nazarbayev said Kazakhstan already ranked second among post-communist states according to per capita direct foreign investment.

He said the resource-rich Central Asian state had received over $6 billion in direct foreign investment and set up over 2,000 joint ventures with foreign firms. Investment commitments in Kazakhstan totalled another $60 billion.
Nazarbayev said the development of Kazakhstan's huge natural reserves, with an estimated value of $8.7 trillion, could be one of the most profitable businesses for foreigners.

Chevron -- one of the largest investors in Kazakhstan -- is already involved in a $20 billion venture to develop the giant Tengiz oil field in western Kazakhstan with estimated reserves of six to nine billion barrels of crude.

"Is it wise to invest in Kazakhstan? Is it safe to invest in Kazakhstan? Speaking from the prospective of Chevron Corp, I can tell you now that the answer...is a resounding 'yes'," Chevron chairman Kenneth Derr told the summit.
Kazakhstan plans to complete sell-offs of its oil and gas companies to strategic investors by July but Nazarbayev said other industries were also waiting for development.
He said Kazakh deposits of copper, lead, zinc, iron, chrome ores, manganese and uranium were among the largest in the world.
Other good spheres for investment were transport and communications, as well as agriculture with an estimated export potential of $25-30 billion a year, he added.
But the president admitted that many foreign investors were scared off by widespread corruption among Kazakh officials.
He pledged to set up a special advisory body of businesses working in Kazakhstan, which will propose changes in investment legislation and inform about bureaucrats extorting bribes from investors.
"In case of bribe-taking, there won't be any protection for any official," he promised.
The attraction of foreign capital and radical market reforms are not welcomed by many ordinary Kazakhs, whose low living standards have brought sympathy for local leftist parties.
But Nazarbayev, who enjoys sweeping executive powers and tolerates little dissent, tried to soothe the investors: "We will never return to the Soviet totalitarian colonial regime."
